steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for a paper proposing consistency models as a policy representation for deep reinforcement learning. Cover existing policy parameterizations, why diffusion policies are expressive but slow, and what we do across offline, offline-to-online and online RL.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Policy parameterization in DRL: discrete vs. continuous, multi-modal representations
- Desiderata for policy representation; diffusion policies and their sampling cost
- Consistency models as a fast alternative
- Our approach: Consistency-BC and Consistency-AC, three RL settings, findings

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Policy parameterization
  - important component of policy-based DRL
  - discrete: Softmax action preferences, Gumbel-Softmax (categorical), decision trees
  - continuous: typically unimodal Gaussian
  - demonstration data often from mixture of behavior policies -> multi-modality
  - GMM, VAE, DDPM used as policy representation
- Desiderata
  - 1. expressiveness: critical for multi-modal data in offline RL / imitation learning (IL)
  - 2. differentiability for SGD
  - 3. computational/time efficiency of sampling, for agents learning from interaction
  - diffusion policies expressive for multi-modal actions; more expressive than GMM/VAE with large sampling steps
  - but progressive denoising over many steps -> slow sampling
  - action inference a bottleneck for online RL (depends on sampling from environments)
  - policy gradient through diffusion nets for all steps: time + memory, not scalable
- Consistency models
  - based on probability flow ODE
  - comparable performance to diffusion, much less compute; few-step generation, faster inference
- Our work
  - first to use consistency model as policy representation for DRL
  - Consistency-BC (behavioral cloning), Consistency-AC (actor-critic)
  - settings: offline, offline-to-online, online; compared with diffusion on D4RL
  - offline: new loss scaling to stabilize training with policy regularization
  - BC with expressive model beats some previous offline RL methods; AC + regularization avoids out-of-distribution actions
  - faster sampling: training time reduced e.g. by 43\% for offline BC; faster action inference online
  - offline-to-online and online: comparable or higher than diffusion in some tasks, much less wall-clock time
  - source code available

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Parameterized policy representation is an important part of policy-based deep reinforcement learning (DRL). Many policy parameterization methods have been developed in prior work. For discrete action spaces, existing parameterizations include Softmax action preferences, Gumbel-Softmax for categorical distributions, decision trees, and others. For continuous action spaces, the most typical choice is a unimodal Gaussian distribution. But in practice the demonstration dataset often has samples from a mixture of behavior policies. To capture the multi-modality in the data distribution, the Gaussian mixture model (GMM), variational auto-encoders (VAE) and the denoising diffusion probabilistic model (DDPM) have been used as policy representations.

There are several things we want from a policy representation in DRL: 1. The function class needs strong expressiveness, which is found to be critical for modeling multi-modal data distributions in offline RL or imitation learning (IL); 2. The model usually has to be differentiable so it is easy to optimize with stochastic gradient descent; 3. Sampling has to be efficient in computation and time, which can be essential for RL agents that learn from interactions with environments. Previous works with action diffusion models (i.e., diffusion policy) show that diffusion models are expressive for multi-modal action distributions. GMM and VAE also capture multi-modality, but diffusion models with large sampling steps are found to be more expressive for IL and offline RL. However, it is known that diffusion models, which denoise progressively over a large number of steps, sample slowly. Action inference can be a critical bottleneck for online RL, which heavily depends on sampling from environments. If diffusion policies are used directly in online settings with policy gradient for optimization, backpropagation has to go through the diffusion networks for the number of sampling steps, and this is not scalable because it takes a lot of time and memory. Consistency models, based on the probability flow ordinary differential equation (ODE), are proposed as a rescue. They have performance comparable to diffusion models but need much less computational time, since they allow a few-step generation process, so the time at inference is significantly reduced.

- Consistency models
  - based on probability flow ODE; comparable performance to diffusion, much less computation
  - few-step generation -> less time at inference
- Our work
  - consistency model as policy representation for DRL (first step)
  - Consistency-BC and Consistency-AC
  - offline, offline-to-online, online; diffusion vs. consistency on D4RL
  - offline: new loss scaling for stability under policy regularization; BC with expressive models beats some offline RL methods; AC + regularization avoids out-of-distribution actions
  - training time reduced (e.g. 43\% for offline BC), faster action inference online
  - offline-to-online / online: comparable or higher than diffusion in some tasks, much shorter wall-clock time
  - code available

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Parameterized policy representation is an important part of policy-based deep reinforcement learning (DRL). Many policy parameterization methods have been developed in prior work. For discrete action spaces, existing parameterizations include Softmax action preferences, Gumbel-Softmax for categorical distributions, decision trees, and others. For continuous action spaces, the most typical choice is a unimodal Gaussian distribution. But in practice the demonstration dataset often has samples from a mixture of behavior policies. To capture the multi-modality in the data distribution, the Gaussian mixture model (GMM), variational auto-encoders (VAE) and the denoising diffusion probabilistic model (DDPM) have been used as policy representations.

There are several things we want from a policy representation in DRL: 1. The function class needs strong expressiveness, which is found to be critical for modeling multi-modal data distributions in offline RL or imitation learning (IL); 2. The model usually has to be differentiable so it is easy to optimize with stochastic gradient descent; 3. Sampling has to be efficient in computation and time, which can be essential for RL agents that learn from interactions with environments. Previous works with action diffusion models (i.e., diffusion policy) show that diffusion models are expressive for multi-modal action distributions. GMM and VAE also capture multi-modality, but diffusion models with large sampling steps are found to be more expressive for IL and offline RL. However, it is known that diffusion models, which denoise progressively over a large number of steps, sample slowly. Action inference can be a critical bottleneck for online RL, which heavily depends on sampling from environments. If diffusion policies are used directly in online settings with policy gradient for optimization, backpropagation has to go through the diffusion networks for the number of sampling steps, and this is not scalable because it takes a lot of time and memory. Consistency models, based on the probability flow ordinary differential equation (ODE), are proposed as a rescue. They have performance comparable to diffusion models but need much less computational time, since they allow a few-step generation process, so the time at inference is significantly reduced.

This paper takes the first step in adapting the consistency model, an expressive and also efficient generative model, as a policy representation for DRL. We put the consistency policy into both a behavioral cloning (BC) method and an actor-critic (AC) algorithm, which we call Consistency-BC and Consistency-AC. We evaluate in three typical RL settings: offline, offline-to-online and online. In all three settings we thoroughly compare policies with two generative models, diffusion model and consistency model, on the D4RL dataset. For offline RL, we propose a new loss scaling to stabilize training of the consistency policy with policy regularization, and we demonstrate that both generative policy models are expressive. We show this by showing that BC with an expressive model like diffusion or consistency gives fairly good policies that outperform some previous offline RL methods. Performance is further improved by using the actor-critic style algorithm with the necessary policy regularization so that out-of-distribution actions are not generated. Because the consistency policy samples fast, it reduces training time, e.g., by 43\% for offline BC, and more importantly it improves time efficiency for online interaction in the environments by making action inference faster. In the offline-to-online setting, where models are initialized by training on the offline dataset, and in the online setting, where learning is from scratch, the consistency policy has comparable or even higher performance than the diffusion policy in some tasks, and it uses significantly shorter wall-clock time for training and inference. The source code is available.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Parameterized policy representation is an important component of policy-based deep reinforcement learning (DRL) [1,2,3]. Prior works have developed a variety of policy parameterization methods. For discrete action spaces, existing policy parameterizations include Softmax action preferences [1], Gumbel-Softmax for categorical distributions [4], decision trees [5,6], etc. For continuous action spaces, the most typical choice is a unimodal Gaussian distribution. In practice, however, the demonstration dataset often contains samples from a mixture of behavior policies. To capture the multi-modality in the data distribution, the Gaussian mixture model (GMM) [7,8], variational auto-encoders (VAE) [9,10] and the denoising diffusion probabilistic model (DDPM) [11,12,13,14,15,16] have been adopted as policy representations.

The desiderata for policy representation in DRL include: 1. Strong expressiveness of the function class, which is found to be critical for modeling multi-modal data distributions in offline RL [13] or imitation learning (IL) [14]; 2. Differentiability of the model, usually required for ease of optimization with stochastic gradient descent; 3. Computational and time efficiency of sampling, which can be essential for RL agents learning from interactions with environments. Previous works with action diffusion models (i.e., diffusion policy) attest to the expressiveness of diffusion models for multi-modal action distributions [13,14,15,17,18]. Although GMM and VAE also capture multi-modality, diffusion models with large sampling steps are found to be more expressive in IL and offline RL scenarios [13,14]. However, it is known that progressive denoising over a large number of steps makes sampling from diffusion models slow. Action inference can be a critical bottleneck for online RL, which heavily depends on sampling from environments. Directly using diffusion policies in online settings with policy gradient for optimization requires backpropagating through the diffusion networks for the number of sampling steps, which is not scalable due to its large time consumption and memory occupancy. Consistency models [19], based on the probability flow ordinary differential equation (ODE), have been proposed as a rescue: they achieve performance comparable to diffusion models with much less computational time, allowing a few-step generation process that significantly reduces time consumption at the inference stage.

This paper takes the first step in adapting the consistency model, an expressive yet efficient generative model, as a policy representation for DRL. The consistency policy is embedded in both a behavioral cloning (BC) method and an actor-critic (AC) algorithm, namely Consistency-BC and Consistency-AC. The experimental evaluation covers three typical RL settings: offline, offline-to-online and online. Policies with two generative models, diffusion model and consistency model, are thoroughly compared in all three settings on the D4RL dataset [20]. For offline RL, we propose a new loss scaling to stabilize the training of the consistency policy with policy regularization, and demonstrate the expressiveness of both generative policy models. This is shown by BC with an expressive model like diffusion or consistency providing fairly good policies that outperform some previous offline RL methods. Performance is further improved by an actor-critic style algorithm with the necessary policy regularization to avoid generating out-of-distribution actions. The fast sampling of the consistency policy not only reduces training time, e.g., by 43\% for offline BC, but more importantly improves time efficiency for online interaction with the environments by accelerating action inference. In the offline-to-online setting, with models initialized by training on the offline dataset, and in the online setting, learning from scratch, the consistency policy shows comparable or even higher performance than the diffusion policy in some tasks, while using significantly shorter wall-clock time for training and inference. The source code is available.
